title: the Alvar hymns
hook: God appears in the sky over a city, and the old devotee's first worry is that someone might put the evil eye on him

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Alvar hymns, three strangers in the rain lit a lamp as big as the world and a lamp made of love. Where did you make room instead of pushing? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.
screen: `TWO LAMPS IN THE DARK.` · `TODAY: A BLESSING FOR GOD.`

segments.voice: A grandmother sees a beautiful baby in the street and, before anything else, says a quick word against the evil eye. Too much praise, the old worry goes, and something bad might follow. Now hold that instinct, and move it. The Sri Vaishnava tradition tells of a temple garland-maker named Vishnuchitta who, on a day of great honor, looked up and saw Vishnu himself in the sky, riding the eagle Garuda, come to watch. Crowds everywhere. And the old man's first feeling wasn't awe, or a request. It was worry. Someone might cast the evil eye on him. So he did what that grandmother does. He sang a blessing over God.
screen: `A WORD AGAINST THE EVIL EYE.` → `VISHNU IN THE SKY.` → `THE OLD MAN WORRIES FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: The blessing is the Tiruppallandu, and its key word is pallandu, many years. Many years, many years, the song begins, to your holy feet. Then the blessing spreads: many years to the goddess at your side, to the wheel and to the conch. It's what you sing over a child or an elder you love. And it's sung to the Lord of the universe. Tradition says that's why Vishnuchitta came to be called Periyalvar, the great Alvar. Tradition says he was also the one who found and raised Andal, whose dawn vow we heard two days ago, so a father and a daughter both sit among the Alvars. His longer hymns keep the same tenderness. In them he sings as Yashoda, Krishna's foster mother: rocking the cradle, coaxing the toddler to come for his bath, calling the moon down to play with him. God as a little one who needs looking after. Hindu teachers have a word for this kind of love: vatsalya, a parent's love, given back to God. A prayer can bring God a need. Periyalvar brings God his care. Love, in these hymns, isn't only receiving protection; it's wanting to protect. A small worry from a big heart, and Sri Vaishnavas still sing it.
screen: `PALLANDU: MANY YEARS.` · `A BLESSING SUNG OVER GOD.` · `SINGING AS YASHODA.` · `LOVE THAT WANTS TO PROTECT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless, instead of ask. Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone you love, and see them clearly, their face, their hands. Now, instead of wanting anything from them, wish them long life. Many years, many years. Let the wish travel with the breath, out toward them, again and again. If another person comes to mind, bless them too. If you pray, you can let the blessing rise toward the name you pray to, the way Periyalvar did. The bell holds the time.
The Alvar hymns. Today, Periyalvar's many years: a blessing sung over God, and the love of a parent given back to the divine. Today's word.
Your line: the Alvar hymns. Today, before asking anyone for anything, give them one quiet blessing first: many years. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas sing Periyalvar's Tiruppallandu in their temples and homes as a blessing over the Lord, alongside Periyalvar's songs of Yashoda and the child Krishna.

pairs: a parent's love, given to God

notes: The hook tells the Vishnuchitta story briefly as tradition (the honor at the Pandya court is left vague on purpose; the debate and the bag of gold are omitted). Confirm.
Tradition holds that the Tiruppallandu opens the Sri Vaishnava recitation of the Alvar hymns; the script says only that Sri Vaishnavas still sing it. A Keeper may want to add its place back.
'The tradition gave Vishnuchitta a new name for it: Periyalvar': the link between the blessing and the name is traditional; confirm the framing.
Contents of the Yashoda songs (cradle, bath, butter, calling the moon) are paraphrased from memory; confirm each.
The cradle and bath songs are attributed to Periyalvar Tirumoli 1–2; confirm the verse ranges if cited more precisely.
Tamil spelling பல்லாண்டு and the stress in 'say' should be checked.

Editor: fixed 'the girl of yesterday's dawn vow' (Andal was day 1222, two days back); the blessing now follows the hymn's order (verse 1 to the holy feet, verse 2 to the Goddess, wheel and conch) and the source ref was widened to 1–2; 'butter on his face' was cut as unsourced; the Periyalvar name is framed as tradition; the stock 'here's why it matters' was cut.
